newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German tax cuts could threaten EMU goals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German tax cuts could threaten EMU goals.

text.p: Germany's cross-party talks on tax reforms risk sacrificing compliance with the terms for economic and monetary union (EMU) by promising tax cuts without matching spending savings, a top economic advisor warned on Wednesday.

Rolf Peffekoven, a member of the "five wise men" panel of independent economists, said more spending cuts or an increase in value-added tax would be needed to pay for Finance Minister Theo Waigel's proposed 30 billion marks ($18 billion) tax-cutting package.
"The politicians are promising tax cuts. It would be honest of them to tell us where they plan to cut spending," Peffekoven told ZDF television.
The alternative -- more borrowing -- would put meeting the Maastricht treaty's fiscal criteria into jeopardy, he added.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party alliance on Monday began talks with opposition Social Democrat (SPD) leaders to try and agree reforms to combat unemployment at 4.7 million -- the highest since the 1930s.

A compromise could bring forward pump-priming tax cuts to next year. Failure would send the project into parliament, where the SPD could block changes in the upper house and turn taxes into a 1998 general election campaign issue.

The chief tax negotiator from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), Wolfgang Schaeuble, urged both sides to reach a quick agreement -- not just on taxes but also on planned reforms to the German state pensions scheme.
"With today's unemployment, no party can afford to think only tactically," Schaeuble told the Die Woche weekly. "Whoever has been caught doing that was always punished by the voters."
Waigel has already said he needs SPD compliance to pass savings measures blocked in parliament to meet the Maastricht budget deficit ceiling of three percent of GDP this year.
The SPD has opposed coalition suggestions for a one-point rise in Germany's 15 percent rate of value-added tax to finance big cuts in personal and corporate taxation over two years.
But Peffekoven warned: "Whoever does not want that must discuss alternatives: either to scrap more tax privileges or not to cut taxes as much."
He also said an SPD proposal to instead raise petrol taxes would brake the economy and exacerbate the jobs crisis -- something the powerful industry lobby also rejected.
"We are for neither an increase in petrol taxes nor VAT -- but clearly for savings," Franz Schoser, chief executive of the Federation of Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), said.

The two sides meet again on Friday in a six-strong working group, and negotiators see scope for an initial compromise on cutting the main corporate tax rate to 35 from 47 percent and trimming labour overheads.

Number-crunchers from both sides also largely cleared a 30 billion mark discrepancy in their calculations of the impact of Waigel's tax plan on Tuesday. But they still disagree on how much income tax cuts would cost, the Finance Ministry said.
The cross-party cooperation on taxes could be tripped up by a separate row over abolishing a capital trading tax which will go to a vote in the Bundestag lower house on Friday.
SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said the government's bill, which would compensate local governments by giving them a share of turnover tax, "clearly violates the constitution".
After a two-year battle, the SPD has vowed to vote down the required constitutional changes -- which require a two-thirds majority in parliament.
Despite signs of compromise on the main reforms, pundits have taken a dim view of Bonn's game of high-stakes tax poker.
"The coalition is shredding its own reform, the opposition is stonewalling, the population is unsettled and trade unions are on the barricades," the Handelsblatt financial daily wrote.
"The chances are becoming ever smaller that, at the end of the negotiation marathon, signals will be set which strengthen enterprise and give Germany a desperately-needed jobs boost."
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.670 German Marks)
